list.listitem: The American Association of Poison Control Centers (AAPCC) has documented over 2 million toxic exposures annually for the past 10 years. Intentional exposures accounted for only 8% of the total exposures, but were responsible for 80% to 90% of the deaths.
In 2015, 93% of human exposures reported to poison control centers occurred at the residence. Approximately 67% of these exposures were treated at the exposure site.
Analgesics was the most frequently involved in human exposures, acounting for 11.1% of the total exposures in 2015.

The array and severity of symptoms reported by the poisoned patient can be helpful in determining the need for further evaluation, interventions, or admission. Note, however, that symptoms and signs may be delayed in some poisonings (eg, acetaminophen), or be masked by a polysubstance exposure.C
Routine comprehensive toxicology screens, except in a few occasions, have not been found to be very helpful in the acute management of the poisoned patient.C

The primary goals in the acute management of the poisoned patient are: (1) to provide immediate supportive care (ie, airway, breathing, circulation); (2) to prevent further absorption of the toxin (ie, decontamination); and (3) if available, to administer an antidote.C
When appropriate, treat all lethargic or comatose patients empirically with the "Coma Cocktail" of dextrose, thiamine, and naloxone (it may require multiple doses).C

Despite the lack of strong evidence for its benefits, activated charcoal as a single dose (1 g/kg or usually 50 g orally) has become the first-line agent in toxin decontamination. Note that airway protection is critically vital when giving charcoal.C

The use of activated charcoal continues to decline, in 2015 activated charcoal was only use in 1.97% of the exposures. The use of ipecac is no longer recommended in all age groups.In general there has been a decline in all methods of decontanimation (activated charcoal, cathartic, ipeccac, lavage, whole body irrigation).
In cases of intentional poisoning, a psychiatric evaluation is recommended after the patient is medically cleared.B
Since 1983, the AAPCC has compiled information reported by regional poison control centers into a national database.
The AAPCC has documented over 2 million toxic exposures annually for the past 10 years and that trend continues.
Approximately 90% of the toxic exposures happen at a residence.
Children under the age of 6 years account for 50% of the exposures, but only 2.3% of the reported deaths.These numbers have remain essentially the same since 1985.
Most exposures (84%) were accidental and involved a single substance.
Intentional exposures (usually by multiple substances) accounted for only 8% of the total, but were responsible for 80% to 90% of the deaths.

A systematic review found that the lifetime prevalence of a witnessed overdose among drug users ranges from 50% to 96%, with a median prevalence of 70%, and of them personally experiencing a nonfatal overdose is 47%.

From 2010 to 2014, the number of drug overdose death increased by 23%. The most frequent mentioned drugs involved in these death were the opioids: Heroine, oxycodone, methadone, morphine, hydrocodone, and fentanyl.
In 2017, 70,237 persons in the United States died of a drug overdose. Two-thirds of these deaths were caused by opiates.

Surveillance data from Europe found that the most common recreational drugs implicated in unintentional overdose were (in order) heroin, cocaine, cannabis, GHB/GBL, and amphetamine. Of 27 fatalities in 5529 patients, half were caused by opioids.

Most reported poisonings are of a minor nature, usually involving a single identified substance. The most common causes of fatal poisonings are shown in . This lists dates from 2005, and more recently opioid overdose has become more common.

The history given by a patient who intentionally overdoses or is intoxicated is unreliable and must be corroborated by EMS personnel, family, friends, health care provider, pharmacist, or medical record.
Ask who, what, how much, when, where, and why, to obtain the following information: age, weight, substance taken, amount, route, time, location, and if accidental or intentional.
Obtain a detailed past medical history, with special emphasis on prior mental illness, suicide attempts, and substance abuse, as well as current medications and allergies.

The array and severity of symptoms reported by the poisoned patient can be helpful in determining the need for further evaluation, interventions, or admission. Note, however, that symptoms and signs may be delayed in some poisonings (eg, acetaminophen), or be masked by a polysubstance exposure.
shows signs and symptoms of common poisoning syndromes.

In one study of children exposed to organophosphate or carbamate insecticide, the presence of pinpoint pupils and diarrhea identified all of the patients with a resource-requiring course but only 7 of 30 patients with a non-resource-requiring course (sensitivity 1.00; 95% CI, 0.95-1.00; specificity 0.77; 95% CI, 0.58-0.90).
Routine comprehensive toxicology screens are generally not helpful in the acute management of the poisoned patient.

Even though use of the stat qualitative urine assays for drugs of abuse has become routine, its value in the patient with acute poisoning continues to be intensely debated. The concerns at this time are: (1) lack of accuracy; (2) lack of impact on acute patient management; and (3) the fact that a positive result in the urine may be completely incidental to the presentation.

There is less debate over routine testing for acetaminophen, on the grounds that a significant number of patients are asymptomatic on initial presentation or are unaware of the ingestion of acetaminophen.
Obtain a pregnancy test when indicated.

Serum electrolytes, glucose, BUN, and creatinine, when used to calculate the anion gap or the osmolar gap, may provide some useful information in suspected poisoning from salicylate, ethanol, ethylene glycol, methanol, and isopropanol.
An ECG can be very helpful in the diagnosis and treatment of cyclic antidepressants, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, and digoxin poisonings.
Chest radiographs and plain abdominal films are of limited value except in patients suspected of aspiration, pulmonary edema, or "drug-packets" ingestion.

The primary goals in the acute management of the poisoning patient are: (1) to provide immediate supportive care (ie, airway, breathing, circulation); (2) to prevent further absorption of the toxin (ie, decontamination); and (3) if available, to administer an antidote.

In the lethargic or comatose patient with a Glasgow Coma Score of less than 8, protect the airway with a cuffed endotracheal tube and assist the breathing. Note that C-spine injuries need to be ruled out in these patients.

When appropriate, treat all lethargic or comatose patients empirically with the "Coma Cocktail": Dextrose 0.5 to 1 g/kg up to 25 g (50 mL) of 50% solution Thiamine 100 mg IV Naloxone 0.2 to 0.4 mg IV; if no response, give 1 to 2 mg IV.
Hypotension is initially treated with IV normal saline. If aggressive fluid replacement fails to bring the blood pressure up, norepinephrine may be required.
Consult with the regional Poison Control Center. The universal telephone number in the United States is 800-222-1222.
Take home noloxone is effective for illicitly manufactured fentanyl and analogs. Higher dose or multiple administrations are often needed.

Despite a lack of strong evidence for its benefits, activated charcoal as a single dose (1 g/kg or usually 50 g orally) has become the first-line agent in toxin decontamination. Note that airway protection is critically vital when giving charcoal.

In a meta-analysis of studies of activated charcoal given to healthy volunteers, administration within 5 minutes of drug ingestion reduced median drug exposure by 88.4% (25-75 percentile: 65.0-96.8); the effect continued to be statistically significant up to 4 hours after drug intake (median reduction in drug exposure 27.4% (range 21.3%-31.5%; P = 0.0006).

Consider multidose activated charcoal (0.5 g/kg every 2-4 hours for at least three doses) only if a patient has ingested a life-threatening amount of carbamazepine, phenobarbital, theophylline, or dapsone.
Activated charcoal is not effective for caustics, ethanol, ethylene glycol, methanol, iron, lithium, metals, and petroleum distillates ingestions.
Routine whole bowel irrigation is not recommended, but may be useful for toxins that are not absorbed by charcoal, and in "drug-packing" decontaminations.
Currently, ipecac and gastric lavage have a very limited role, if any, in the management of the poisoned patient.
Effective antidotes are available for a limited number of toxins and when indicated, they should be administered (see ).
In a recent study of poisoned patients treated in the emergency department, 77% were medically cleared to be safely discharged home after just 2 to 4 hours' observation.
Consider hospitalization for symptomatic patients who have ingested potentially fatal medications.

Consider ICU admission in patients with the following high-risk criteria: Need for intubation Seizures Unresponsive to verbal stimuli Arterial carbon dioxide pressure of 45 mmHg or greater Any rhythm except sinus arrhythmia Second- or third-degree AV block or QRS greater than 0.12 seconds In cyclic antidepressant poisoning, a QRS greater than 0.10 seconds and sign(s) of toxicity Systolic blood pressure less than 80 mm Hg
In cases of intentional poisoning, a psychiatric evaluation is required after the patient is medically cleared.

Education and advocating for safer products and child-resistant containers have greatly reduced the numbers of pediatric poisonings. Note that in 2015, 93% of exposures reporeded to poison centers occurrred at a residence.

In a meta-analysis of the effectiveness of home safety education and the provision of safety equipment, investigators found increased rates of safe storage of medicines (OR 1.57; 95% CI, 1.22, 2.02) and cleaning products (OR 1.63; 95% CI, 1.22, 2.17), the possession of syrup of ipecac (OR 3.34; 95% CI, 1.50, 7.41), and having poison control numbers accessible (OR 3.67; 95% CI, 1.84, 7.33) but no clear evidence of reduced poisoning rates.

Even though relatively small numbers of pediatric poisonings are referred to health care facilities, these visits may afford an opportune time for staff to educate caregivers about poisoning prevention.
Household interventions are ineffective in reducing blood lead levels in children.

Give the following information to caregivers: Keep potential poison out of sight and reach. Always reengage child-resistant closure in the locked mode immediately after using the pharmaceutical or consumer product. Never transfer a substance from its original to an alternate container. Safely dispose of all unused and no-longer-needed medications. Do not refer to medicines as "candy". Post the poison control center number near the telephone (1-800-222-1222).

feature.caption: Antidotes for Common Poisonings.
feature.feature_body:
Substance Antidote Dose
Acetaminophen N-acetylcysteine Loading dose: 140 mg/kg orally or 150 mg/kg IV over 1 hour
Maintenance: 70 mg/h orally every 4 h x 17 doses or 50 mg/kg IV infusion x4 hours, then 100 mg/kg x16 hours 0.2 mg IV over 30 seconds
Benzodiazepines Flumazenil Then 0.3-0.5 mg every 30 seconds as needed up to 3 mg total
Do not use in chronic benzodiazepine use or in cyclic antidepressant overdose 0.05 mg/kg IV bolus; may repeat in 10 minutes
Beta-blockers Glucagon Then IV infusion of 0.07 mg/kg/h 1 g calcium chloride IV (adults)
Calcium channel blockers Calcium, glucagons 20-30 mg/kg/dose (children)
Glucagon same as above 100% oxygen
Carbon monoxide Oxygen Consider hyperbaric oxygen in severe cases
Cyanide Cyanide antidote kit, Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) Induce methemoglobinemia with inhaled amyl nitrite 0.3 mL followed by sodium nitrate 300 mg IV over 2-4 minutes
Then administer sodium thiosulfate 12.5 g IV
Or Cyanokit 5 g IV; if needed, repeat dose (adults) 44-88 mEq IV push (adults)
Cyclic antidepressants Bicarbonate 44-88 mEq IV push (adults)
1-2 mEq/kg IV push (children)
Digoxin Digoxin-specific antibodies 5-10 vials (digoxin level unknown)
Ethylene glycol Ethanol, fomepizole, thiamine Ethanol (10% mixed in D5W) 1 g/kg, then 1-2 mL/kg/h IV infusion
Or fomepizole 15 mg/kg, then 10 mg/kg q12 h x4
Thiamine 100 mg IV
Iron Deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/h IV
Isoniazid (INH) Pyridoxine g/g INH ingested (max. dose 5 g)
Lead Calcium disodium edetate (EDTA) 1000 mg/m2/d IV infusion (over 8-12 hours)
Methanol Ethanol, fomepizole Same as in ethylene glycol
Opioids Naloxone 0.2-0.4 mg IV; if no response, give 1-2 mg IV
Organophosphate Atropine, pralidoxime Atropine 2-4 mg IV every 5-10 minutes as needed; 0.05 mg/kg IV every 5min as needed (child)
Pralidoxime 1-2 g IV infusion over 15-30 minutes; may repeat dose after 1 hour if needed
